n: This psalm is nearly identical to Psalm 14; the main difference is that it uses “God” (Elohim) instead of “the LORD.” The fool isn’t unintelligent — he lives as if God doesn’t matter.

f.w: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God

f.g: Hebrew nabal — morally senseless, not mentally slow.

n: God looks down from heaven searching for anyone who understands and seeks him.
Everyone has turned back and become corrupt — not a single one does good. Paul quotes these lines to show that all people need God’s grace.

f.w: there is none that doeth good, no, not one

n: Don’t evildoers understand anything? They devour God’s people as casually as eating bread, and never pray.

f.w: eat up my people as they eat bread

n: Here this psalm departs most from Psalm 14: it describes enemies terrified even when there was nothing to fear, as God scattered the bones of the army besieging his people.

f.g: Panic without any visible cause — sent by God.
Left their bodies unburied — total defeat.

n: A longing that salvation would come from Zion. When God restores his people, all Israel will rejoice. Latter-day Saints also see this as a hope fulfilled in the gathering of Israel.

f.g: Restores the fortunes of his people.
